claim: maup's assign() function crosswalks source geometries (e.g. census blocks, precincts) to target geometries (e.g. districts, redrawn precincts) by covering-area rule: a source unit is assigned to whichever target geometry covers the largest portion of its area when it isn't fully covered by one.
stance_target: geospatial crosswalk methodology for reconciling electoral geography across redistricting cycles
scope_conditions: US redistricting data; general spatial-crosswalk technique, portable to any jurisdiction with polygon precinct/block shapefiles
quoted_support: The Series maps each geometry in sources to the geometry in targets that covers it. ... If a source geometry is not covered by one single target geometry, it is assigned to the target geometry that covers the largest portion of its area.

claim: maup's official documentation explicitly warns against prorating election/demographic data by area, since larger census blocks are less populous than smaller ones (correlation runs opposite to naive area-weighting intuition); population-based weights should be used instead.
stance_target: population-weighted (not area-weighted) proration is the correct method for redistributing vote/demographic data across mismatched geographic units
scope_conditions: any areal interpolation of electoral or demographic data between non-nesting precinct/block geometries
quoted_support: We strongly urge you not to prorate by area! The area of a census block is not a good predictor of its population. In fact, the correlation goes in the other direction: larger census blocks are less populous than smaller ones.

claim: In a real-world maup worked example, disaggregating vote totals from old precincts to census blocks and reaggregating to new (redrawn) precinct boundaries lost roughly 12% of Democratic votes (23,401 to 20,566) and 11% of Republican votes (3,302 to 2,947) purely due to boundary mismatch between old-precinct and new-precinct shapefiles -- 884 and 1,227 of 3,014 total blocks respectively were unassigned to any precinct in each shapefile.
stance_target: precinct/bureau-de-vote boundary redrawing between election cycles introduces material data loss/error in crosswalked election results unless topology is explicitly repaired
scope_conditions: Providence, Rhode Island test dataset; illustrative of a general boundary-mismatch failure mode relevant to French bureau-de-vote redecoupage between 2022 and 2027
quoted_support: So, out of 3,014 total Census blocks, 884 were not assigned to any old precinct and 1,227 were not assigned to any new precinct.

claim: maup's smart_repair() function can enforce that repaired precinct geometries nest cleanly within a secondary set of region boundaries (e.g. counties), via the nest_within_regions parameter, addressing the common real-world case where precincts are supposed to nest into higher administrative units but don't due to shapefile stitching artifacts.
stance_target: tooling capability for enforcing administrative-hierarchy consistency in crosswalked geographies (analogous to needing bureau de vote to commune/canton consistency in France)
quoted_support: smart_repair allows the user to optionally specify a second shapefile---e.g., a shapefile of county boundaries within a state---and then performs the repair process so that the repaired geometries nest cleanly into the units in the second shapefile.

claim: The maup package name and design philosophy is explicitly grounded in the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP), the statistical-geography principle that the same underlying spatial data yields different aggregate results depending on how the space is partitioned.
stance_target: theoretical grounding for why bureau-de-vote-level projection methods are sensitive to boundary choice/redecoupage
scope_conditions: general spatial statistics principle, not France-specific
quoted_support: The name of this package comes from the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP): the same spatial data will look different depending on how you divide up the space.
